message.content:
The number of distinct legal positions that can arise in a game of chess is astronomically large – on the order of **10⁴³**.  

This figure, often called the *Shannon number*, was first estimated by Claude Shannon in 1950. It represents an upper bound on the number of possible arrangements of the 32 pieces (including pawns, rooks, knights, bishops, queen, king, and the special pawn‑promotion possibilities) on the 64‑square board, taking into account all the rules that restrict which arrangements are legal (e.g., kings cannot be in check, pawns cannot be on the first or last rank unless promoted, etc.).

For comparison, the number of possible distinct games (i.e., sequences of legal moves from the starting position to any end position) is even larger—roughly **10¹²⁰**. But when people ask about “possible arrangements” they almost always mean the number of legal board positions, which is about 10⁴³.
